text: Hello, this is Mark Wildman of Wildman Athletica and today we're going to talk about two martial get-ups, the Krav get-up and the Judo get-up, sometimes referred to as a technical stand-up. We're going to talk about these two get-ups because if you can't get up off of the ground quickly under stress, you have a hole in your athletic training that you should definitely fill. Normally, the only type of get-ups that people do are burpees. If you do CrossFit, if you're military, you're law enforcement, you do a lot of burpees. Burpees are useful for the military because they tend to be running, they get down on the ground with the gun, they pop up, they start moving forward again. There are a bunch of other types of get-ups that you should work on if you're not military, if you're civilian. We like to focus on the most useful get-ups first, defensive get-ups. Two get-ups that we're working on today, the Krav get-up. The Krav get-up is a defensive get-up where you get knocked down and you get up while facing forward but moving back, and a Judo get-up, which is where you get up from the same spot where you hit the ground, sometimes called a technical stand-up. Both the Krav get-up and the Judo get-up will start from a movement that we call a deck squat or a rear rolling ground engagement. If you practice something like jujitsu or you do throwing in armor, you practice circus arts or gymnastics, you will recognize this movement right away. Getting down, not slamming our skull into the ground, coming to a rested stop, one leg bent, one leg straight, opposite hand goes on the ground as opposite leg so that you can post, lift your hip up, get your hip all the way back. Now, my feet are pointed straight ahead, my hips are pointed straight ahead, and my hands are up. Basic defensive get-up. Get knocked down to the ground, don't slam your skull down, and figure out how to get up in the least amount of time. The Judo get-up, similar base, but instead of moving back, we're going to get up in the same spot. Get down to the ground, don't slam your skull into the ground. Instead of moving all the way back through, we are going to get up in the same spot that we touched down. The problem most people have when they're learning this is that they don't practice it enough. Normally, athletes, even well-trained ones, tend to start around 12 reps in 20 seconds and build up from there.
